introduction.p: An integral over an infinite interval, or with an unbounded integrand near an endpoint or interior point, is defined using limits of integrals over finite nonsingular intervals. It converges when every required limit is finite. This section develops comparison tests and distinguishes absolute convergence from convergence caused by cancellation.

exercise.title: Why can a finite interval still be improper?

statement.p: The integral \int_0^1 x^{-1/2}\,dx lives on a finite interval, but the integrand blows up at 0. In your own words, why must we still approach the endpoint by a limit, and why can a tall spike still enclose finite area?

hint.p: The original definite integral assumes a bounded integrand on a closed interval. A vertical asymptote is a second kind of improperness. Narrow spikes can have finite area even when they are infinitely tall.

subsection.title: Convergence and divergence
subsection.p: The words convergent and divergent describe the limiting process, not the antiderivative.
An improper integral converges if the limiting accumulated amount approaches a finite number. It diverges if the limiting accumulated amount does not approach a finite number.
The antiderivative may exist on every finite subinterval and the improper integral may still diverge.

exercise.title: Why can an antiderivative exist on every finite piece while the improper integral diverges?

statement.p: For every finite t>1, \int_1^t(1/x)\,dx=\ln t exists, but \int_1^\infty(1/x)\,dx diverges. In your own words, why do the words convergent and divergent describe the limiting accumulated amount, not the existence of an antiderivative?

hint.p: Convergence means the running total approaches a finite number. An antiderivative on each compact subinterval is not the same as a finite total for the whole improper accumulation.

exercise.title: Why can comparison decide convergence without finding a value?

statement.p: The integral \int_1^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx has no elementary antiderivative, yet it converges because e^{-x^2}\le e^{-x} for x\ge1. In your own words, why is a smaller nonnegative area finite when a larger comparison area is finite, and why are the p-integrals a useful comparison family?

hint.p: If you already know a larger nonnegative tail has finite area, a smaller tail cannot have infinite area. The power 1/x^p is a catalog of tails whose convergence is settled, so you can match an unknown tail to a known one.

Improper integrals teach a useful discipline. Do not evaluate first and ask questions later. First ask where the integral is improper. Then replace the dangerous endpoint or discontinuity by a limit. Then decide whether the limit is finite.
The next section collects the mistakes this discipline prevents.

subsection.title: Absolute and conditional convergence
subsection.p: Cancellation can make a signed accumulation finite even when the total unsigned area is infinite. An improper integral \int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx is absolutely convergent if \int_a^\infty|f(x)|\,dx converges. It is conditionally convergent if the signed integral converges but the absolute-value integral diverges. Use the same definitions at a singular endpoint, and require convergence on every piece when several endpoints or singularities are involved.

note.title: Absolute convergence implies convergence
note.p: Assume f is continuous on each finite subinterval. Put f_+=\max(f,0) and f_-=\max(-f,0). Both are nonnegative and bounded above by |f|. Comparison shows that their improper integrals converge if the integral of |f| does. Since f=f_+-f_-, the signed integral then converges too. Moreover, for any tail beginning at R,

warning.title: Keep the two tails separate
warning.p: Conditional convergence still requires each improper piece to converge. The symmetric values \int_{-R}^R\sin x\,dx=0 do not make \int_{-\infty}^\infty\sin x\,dx convergent. Such a symmetric limiting procedure is called a Cauchy principal value; it is a different definition.

statement.p: Classify \int_1^\infty\cos x/x\,dx, \int_1^\infty\cos x/x^2\,dx, and \int_0^1\sin(1/x)\,dx as absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent, or divergent.

hint.p: The first is conditional: integrate by parts using the bounded antiderivative \sin x, and adapt the lobe lower bound for |\cos x|. The other two are absolute; bound by 1/x^2 and by 1, respectively.
